The `uptime` command reported load averages of 4.86, 5.77, and 6.02 over the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes, respectively. These figures represent the average number of processes actively executing on a CPU, waiting for CPU time, or suspended in uninterruptible sleep such as disk I/O. Because the 1-minute metric is lower than the 15-minute value, the system is experiencing a slight easing of demand compared to earlier sustained activity.

On a build server, a consistently elevated load average typically signals that compilation jobs and tests are saturating available resources. While parallel compilers like Make, Ninja, and Gradle intentionally push load averages above the physical core count to hide I/O latency, excessively high values lead to severe context-switching overhead and thrashing. If disk or network operations become bottlenecks during artifact generation, processes will accumulate in uninterruptible wait states and drive queue lengths even higher, ultimately extending build durations and causing pipeline delays.

This output reflects a Saturday afternoon in the Eastern Daylight Time zone, exactly four hours behind Coordinated Universal Time. It confirms that the system's local clock is configured with an active timezone offset and is tracking standard wall-clock time.

Server clocks drift over time primarily due to physical imperfections in their quartz crystal oscillators. Variations in ambient temperature, power supply fluctuations, and component aging alter the vibration frequency of these crystals, causing the hardware timer to run slightly faster or slower than real time. To counter this hardware drift and prevent accumulated skew, production systems regularly synchronize their clocks against authoritative reference sources using protocols like NTP or PTP.
